extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of physical/experimental science (physicists, meteorologists, experimentalists) learning measurement, approximation, and quantitative induction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on measurement, treating approximate quantities, inferring empirical/rational laws from numerical data, and principles for neglecting higher-order small effects in physical science. Covers notation, rounding, fitting empirical formulae, and criteria for causal inference from varying quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with linear approximation then progress to higher orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Commence quantitative investigation by discovering linear variation first, and afterwards proceed to elliptic (second-order) or more complicated laws of variation (third, fourth, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict attention to very small portions of a curve where higher-order terms are imperceptible; if larger arcs are considered, fit parabola, ellipse, cubic, etc., successively. The common practice is to begin with simplest (linear) forms and increase complexity only as measurement accuracy warrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent small arcs by low-degree polynomial (parabolas of some order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any smooth portion of a curve may be approximated by an equation y = A + Bx + Cx^2 + ...; for sufficiently small portions higher powers are negligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a parabola (second-order) or higher polynomial of appropriate degree to approximate the curve to the precision of observation; choose the lowest degree that fits observed deviations to avoid overfitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of approximate independence of small effects (superposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: When effects are small compared with observation precision, each cause may be considered as producing its own effect independently; joint effect ≈ sum of separate effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when individual displacements/changes are very small so cross-terms are of higher order and negligible. Examples: Bernoulli's treatment of small vibrations (sound), tidal contributions from moon and sun, linear approximation of gravity variation with small height h. Beware that principle is only approximate — interference can produce secondary effects detectable at higher precision (Helmholtz's resultant tones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect higher-order (product) terms when they are of much smaller magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: If two small fractional changes a and b act together, the combined change (1+a)(1+b)=1+a+b+ab can be approximated by 1+a+b because ab is much smaller and may be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to simplify combined effects (e.g., strains, thermal expansions). Ensure a and b are sufficiently small that the product term is truly negligible; otherwise retain higher-order terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat motions/effects as infinitely small to eliminate interference (differential approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians avoid error by considering motions as infinitely small so interference between forces becomes higher-order infinitesimal and may be neglected; differential calculus models motion as composed of infinitely many infinitesimal diagonals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use infinitesimal/differential reasoning to justify superposition and to derive accurate formulæ when appropriate. In physical science where only perceptible minima exist, check that 'infinitely small' assumption maps to 'imperceptible' for your instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use series expansions for functions when variable << 1 and truncate appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand functions (e.g., (1+h)^{-2}) as power series and truncate higher powers when h is very small so those terms are inappreciable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to derive linear approximations (e.g., gravity variation with height) and to justify replacing exact expressions by simpler approximations. Verify that neglected higher-order terms (h^2, h^3, ...) are below measurement sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply abbreviated algebraic rules for quantities small compared with unity
rubrics_metrics.description: When variable quantity a is very small compared with unity, use substitutions like 1/(1+a) ≈ 1−a; other similar shorthand rules (Kohlrausch's rules) speed calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these approximations to simplify calculations, but be mindful of domain of validity (|a| << 1). Cross-check with full expression if accuracy requirement is tight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish four meanings of equality (absolute, sub-equality, apparent, probable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality may mean absolute (perfect theoretical equality), sub-equality (equal within an infinitesimal), apparent equality (difference imperceptible to senses/instruments), or probable equality (results close enough that differences can be ascribed to unimportant disturbances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'apparent equality' in physical science when differences are below perceptual/instrumental thresholds; treat experimental agreement as 'probable equality' and quantify allowable deviation by probable error limits. Recognize mathematical proofs yield absolute equality, while experiments rarely do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and rules to indicate degree of exactness of decimal numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose notation to express whether a decimal fraction is exact or approximate (e.g., small circle for completely exact .0250; colon or dots to show whether retained figure is rounded up or down). Use De Morgan's rounding rule: if first rejected digit ≥5, raise retained digit by one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt consistent notation to avoid ambiguity about whether given decimals are exact values or intervals. When publishing, indicate whether decimal digits are exact or rounded and by what rule; this reduces misinterpretation of precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: When combining approximate numbers, track accuracy of the result
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) on approximate decimals make it complex to determine resultant accuracy; follow systematic rules (e.g., Sandeman, Sonnenschein & Nesbitt) to handle approximate arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow established procedures for approximate arithmetic to avoid needless labour and to take proper account of inaccuracy. When in doubt, consult standard references on approximate calculations and the method of carrying significant figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unjustified numerical precision (no false precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not display more decimal places than the nature of the data/measurement justifies; giving excessive decimal fractions falsely implies greater accuracy (Leslie's protest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically avoid giving more than one figure of uncertain amount; chemists and others should not publish absurdly many decimals when processes cannot support that precision. Choose number of significant figures that reflect estimated instrument and procedural errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three central questions of quantitative investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: For every important quantitative phenomenon answer: (1) Is there any constant relation between variable and variant? (2) What is the empirical formula expressing this relation? (3) What is the rational formula expressing the law of nature involved?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite framework when moving from raw measurements to laws: first establish correlation/probable connection, fit an empirical mathematical representation, then seek underlying theoretical (rational) explanation. Each stage has differing evidential standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit empirical mathematical laws by low-order polynomials or trigonometric series as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Given paired measurements, one can represent the relation by polynomials y = A + Bx + Cx^2 + ... or by sines/cosines for periodic phenomena; choose number of terms based on desired accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve for constants using three data points for a quadratic, or use method of least squares for best-fit parameters. For periodic phenomena (meteorology, tides) represent the wave by sines and cosines; meteorological series often need only three or four terms. Be mindful of overfitting — include higher powers only when justified by data and accuracy requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use controlled variation (manipulation) to establish causation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a cause can be varied at will and the effect follows in exact temporal coincidence (make/break current, introduce/exhaust air), this synchronous control yields high improbability of casual coincidence and strongly supports causal dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer manipulative experiments to observational coincidence when inferring causation. Historical examples: Faraday's control of electro-magnets affecting light, Tyndall's singing flames. Temporal coincidence in controlled changes is a strong inductive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal coincidence and measurement precision determine probability of causal connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate measurements and mere resemblance of variation give only small probability of connection; near-exact coincidence to infinitely small differences would provide near-certainty but is unattainable — so probabilities are proportional to measurement accuracy and frequency of time coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two quantities vary together, evaluate probability of connection based on precision, frequency, and synchrony of observations. Recognize limits: absolute proof would require infinite measurement precision or infinite observation time; instead aim for sufficiently high probability for scientific purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for eliminating and managing measurement errors
rubrics_metrics.description: All small errors may be assumed to vary approximately proportional to their causes — therefore when eliminating errors make them as small as possible first; error propagation often behaves approximately linearly for very small errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce individual sources of error before combining measurements; use error-reduction methods (Chap. XV referenced) and account for propagation of uncertainty when combining measured quantities. Use logarithmic or other transformations where appropriate to linearize error behaviour.
